Rhizoma Smoke is a growth engine by the Sativus Gourd atelier and the SG Rhizoma typeface family grown with it, led by SG Smoke. It is built on Rhizoma, Dabin Kim’s growing type system for the letters of IM Fell English, and adds Hangul, smoke that climbs out of the letter, roots that join across letters and lines, growth that rises through a text, and seeds that bring any growth back.

Meet the SG Rhizoma Family

SG Smoke, SG Drag, SG Flame and SG Rhizoma V2, with SG Root and SG Tangle as experiments.

01Constant ConnectionRoots that join across letters and lines.
중심 뿌리나 명확한 경계가 없는 이 생장 방식은 디지털 경험을 설명하는 완벽한 은유다.“A rhizome, which spreads horizontally without a central root or clear boundaries, serves as a perfect metaphor for the modern digital experience of infinite connection and entanglement.”Dabin Kim, Rhizoma

In botany, a rhizome is an underground stem that spreads sideways and sprouts new roots at every node. The idea goes back to Deleuze and Guattari’s A Thousand Plateaus, where “any point of a rhizome can be connected to anything other, and must be.”

Rhizoma takes the first half of that sentence. Its roots spread from every letter and cross one another, but each grows from one point to one tip and passes over the rest. Rhizoma Smoke takes the second half: in SG Drag and SG Tangle, a root that comes near another root, letter or line joins it, so a word grows as one body and two lines as one field.

02Gradual ProliferationGrowth that rises letter by letter, and fonts with a Growth axis.

Rhizoma grows every letter of a text at the same growth stage and line weight. In Kim’s zine, a spread of text grows denser from one page to the next, and one A grows through rising stages. Here growth can change along a text: Growth in the SG Rhizoma Engine sets it where the text starts and where it ends, on Rhizoma’s own scale of 0 to 20. SG Rhizoma V2 follows that scale exactly. The other faces are fitted to it, so that 20 is as far as each one grows before its letters are lost. Each of them grows as one plant: a step up keeps every root of the step below and adds more. SG Smoke climbs to a forest of separate stems at 20; in SG Drag, growth goes into the current, with more strands and longer drifts.

A font cannot know where a letter sits on a page, so every core face also comes as a variable font: SG Smoke, SG Drag, SG Flame and SG Rhizoma V2, and SG Root among the experiments. Their Growth axis runs from the bare letter at 0 to the full growth at 100 and can be set per word, line or page in any app that reads variable fonts.

The text is the last line of Voltaire’s Candide, which gave the SG Rhizoma Engine its heading.

04How a Letter GrowsFrom an IM Fell English glyph to one grown outline.

Rhizoma is a browser tool designed and programmed by Dabin Kim, shared on GitHub under a Creative Commons licence. Kim calls it “a growing type system.” It samples points inside each letter of IM Fell English, lets a few of them sprout, walks each root forward in small random turns, lets roots branch, and merges the roots with the letter into one outline that saves as a font or a vector file.

Rhizoma Smoke keeps that sequence. SG Rhizoma V2, in the SG Rhizoma Engine above, runs the original engine at its default settings, so the method and the SG faces can be compared on the same text. The other faces change where a root starts, how it moves and whether it meets anything. In SG Root, below, roots start on the outline and leave along its outward normal, so each one grows straight out of the letter.

IM Fell English is Igino Marini’s digitisation of the Fell Types, the founts Bishop John Fell left to Oxford in 1686. Type historians place them before Caslon, on Dutch models. Marini kept the uneven edges and ink spread of the printed originals, which is why the letter already looks grown.

06Hangul / 한글The 2,350 syllables of KS X 1001, grown from Song Myung.

For an atelier that works in Korean as often as English, Hangul was the first addition. Rhizoma Smoke reads two typefaces as one stack: Latin from IM Fell English and Hangul from Song Myung, an open Myeongjo, the Korean serif tradition. A syllable block holds far more ink than a Latin letter, so every face but SG Rhizoma V2 sprouts Hangul at 0.45 of the Latin rate, and a line of Hangul grows about as densely as a line of Latin.

Hangul’s distinctions are small. One short stroke separates ㅏ from ㅑ, and a tick on top turns ㅈ into ㅊ. A root that leaves a stem in the wrong place can read as a stroke. The lower sprout rate is the first guard: fewer roots per syllable leaves fewer chances to land on a stem. The second is direction. In SG Flame, roots sprout only from edges that face upward and then rise, so no root starts on the side of a vertical stem, where ㅏ would turn into ㅑ and ㅓ into ㅕ.

The third is a guard in SG Root, where every root starts on the outline of a stroke. Once a line has grown, it takes out any Hangul root that leaves its syllable sideways, where the tick of ㅏ or ㅓ sits, and any root whose part outside the letter is short and nearly straight, the tick that turns ㅡ into ㅗ or ㅈ into ㅊ. Every other root stays where it grew, Latin is untouched, and the SG Root font carries the same guard.

Special Thanks to Dabin Kim

Rhizoma Smoke is built upon Rhizoma, the growing type system Dabin Kim released openly under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence, and every face on this page grows by her method. Her zine of the same name, in Korean and English, describes the system.

SG Smoke stays closest to the original: the same sampling and walk, with fewer roots that taper, drift upward and break up as they climb. SG Rhizoma V2 is the original engine at its default settings, with seeds, Hangul, growth that can rise through a text, and fonts that install with kerning and ligatures, one of them with a Growth axis.
